title: To a Coquette
text:
Like those little lights,

vaporous and light,

that without heat by the thousands

rise from the earth,


loves in your breast,

most fragile beauty,

without their fire burning you,

raise a thousand different flames:


they spring up, shine, vanish,

others are born after them:

inconstancy puts them out,

frivolity renews them.
editorial_note: The translation keeps Coronado's comparison between fleeting earth-lights and the coquette's quickly renewed loves.

title: Nothing Remains of You
text:
Nothing remains of you... the abyss sank you...

the monsters of the seas swallowed you.

In those funereal places not even

your own bones are left of you.

Easy to understand, beloved Alberto,

is that you lost your life in the sea,

but the grieving soul cannot understand

how I live when you have died.

To give life to me and death to you;

to give peace to you and war to me,

to leave you in the sea and me on land

is fate's greatest cruelty!!




1848
editorial_note: The translation preserves the elegy's direct accusation against fate after Alberto's death at sea.

title: To a Dewdrop
text:
Living tear of the fresh dawn,

to whom the withered flower owes its life,

and whom the thirsty meadow drinks among the leaves;

drop that the sun gilds with its reflections;


that on the seductive complexion of flowers,

rocked by the lightest zephyr,

mixes your snow color with crimson

and with snow their charming crimson:


come mix yourself with my sad weeping,

and consume yourself on my burning cheek;

for perhaps the bitter tears I swallow


will run more sweetly...

but what would one drop of dew be,

lost in the torrent of my tears...!
editorial_note: The translation keeps the sonnet's motion from dawn dew and flowers into the speaker's overwhelming tears.

title: The White Rose
text:
Which of the daughters of burning summer,

candid rose, equals your beauty,

the softest complexion and the freshness

that spring from your shining face?


The rosy light of newborn dawn

shows no greater sweetness as it opens,

nor the wing of swans the whiteness

of the pilgrim circle of your brow.


Thus, glory of the garden, in the splendid

cluster you stand out from your green seat;

when, carried on the gentle wind,


to your fragrant silver chalice

a licentious insect steals its aroma,

and clouds the pure enamel with its breath.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the white rose's idealized purity and the final disturbance by the insect.

title: How I Adore You!
text:
Oh, how I adore you! with the light of day

I invoke your name, impassioned and sad,

and when the sky dresses itself in shadows,

my exalted soul still calls to you.


You are the time that guides my hours,

you are the idea that attends my mind,

because in you is concentrated all that exists,

my passion, my hope, my poetry.


There is no song that can equal your accent

when you tell me of your love and rave,

revealing the faith of your contentment;


I tremble at your voice and tremble if you look at me,

and I would like to exhale my last breath

burning in the air you breathe.




1845
editorial_note: The translation keeps Coronado's sonnet as a concentrated declaration of passionate devotion.
